thread.title: New cholesterol guidelines aim to stop heart disease earlier
thread.title_full: New cholesterol guidelines aim to stop heart disease earlier

author: First State Times
title: New cholesterol guidelines aim to stop heart disease earlier
text:
Doctors should consider treating high cholesterol much earlier and more aggressively than before, according to a May 20 perspective by investigators from Weill Cornell Medicine, NewYork-Presbyterian, and Yale School of Medicine. The updated 2026 cholesterol management guidelines from the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association encourage doctors to identify risk sooner and intervene before heart attacks or strokes occur.
The new approach is significant because heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States. By focusing on prevention at an earlier stage, medical professionals hope to reduce the number of serious cardiovascular events.
The perspective, published May 19 in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, highlights both opportunities and challenges for primary care clinicians in implementing these recommendations. “Primary care clinicians are really the backbone of patient care, especially when it comes to cardiovascular prevention. Due to our longitudinal relationships with patients we are uniquely positioned to reinforce healthy behaviors related to diet, exercise, sleep and smoking,” said Dr. Madeline R. Sterling, associate professor of medicine at Weill Cornell and an internist at NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center. She added that primary care clinicians can screen patients earlier for lifetime cardiovascular risk factors and manage abnormal blood fat levels more effectively.
Dr. Erica S. Spatz, associate professor of cardiology and epidemiology at Yale School of Medicine, also co-authored the perspective.
In previous years, treatment decisions often focused on whether someone was likely to have a heart attack or stroke within ten years. Now experts say even younger adults with moderately elevated cholesterol may benefit from intervention if they carry other hidden risks. The guidelines recommend using newer tools such as measuring lipoprotein(a), a genetically inherited particle linked to heart disease, as well as coronary artery calcium scans that detect silent plaque buildup.
The recommendations include starting statin medication earlier alongside lifestyle changes if necessary but acknowledge practical challenges in busy clinics where time is limited for discussing complex risks with patients.
Experts warn that without careful implementation these advances could widen existing health disparities since some tests or medications may not be available everywhere or covered by insurance plans.
Drs. Sterling and Spatz say successful adoption will require better insurance coverage options for advanced testing and medications along with improved electronic health record systems, expanded patient education efforts, research support for best practices implementation—and stronger collaboration between primary care providers and specialists.
The guidelines also promote team-based approaches involving nurses or pharmacists helping patients reach their targets safely over time through coordinated efforts among all members involved in patient care.
